newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Fuming and feuding the custom in Israeli politics.
newsitem.headline: Fuming and feuding the custom in Israeli politics.

text.p: First Lady Sara Netanyahu's videotaped temper tantrum this week underscores the passions that race through public discourse in Israel like blasts of heat across the Middle East sands.

Bristling when asked about husband Benjamin Netanyahu's extra-marital affair, Sara slammed her predecessor Sonia Peres for staying at home, accused legislators of making passes at her and then halted the television interview, witnesses said.
The taping at Israel's Channel One only resumed on a promise to delete the outbursts when the interview airs on Sunday.

The comments may have exceeded usual norms -- Mrs Netanyahu has been at the heart of several controversies in the year since her husband became prime minister -- but the contentiousness is customary in a small, politicised country where familiarity at times breeds contempt and people's emotions are quick to boil under a Mediterranean sun.

Visitors accustomed to closed-mouth societies say they find it hard getting used to everyone wanting to talk -- even if the subject is not something weighty, such as whether Israel should swap land for peace with the Arabs.

"It still is a very politicised society on very fundamental issues. It's also polarised -- a very passionate society," said Yossi Olmert, an activist in Netanyahu's Likud party and former Government Press Office director.

News of the first lady's interview surfaced in the tabloids on Thursday. Later in the day her husband, besieged by criticism of his performance in office, became locked in a war of words with newly installed Labour opposition leader Ehud Barak.
Barak said the prime minister's dead brother -- a military hero in Israel -- would be ashamed of him today. Netanyahu retaliated by telling supporters: "I heard a small slander from a little man."
For Israelis, name-calling -- or something like it -- is an integral part of politics.
Israel's founding father David Ben-Gurion refused even to call opposition leader Menachem Begin by his name, referring to him only as "that man who sits next to Knesset member Bader."
The late Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin made peace with the Palestinians and Jordan but when at war with rival politicians, he would paste nicknames on them that stuck for life.
He once labelled his Labour party rival Shimon Peres an "indefatiguable schemer" and gave the moniker "Peres's poodle" to Labour party activist Yossi Beilin.

Before his assassination 20 months ago Rabin himself came under verbal attack from opponents of his land-for-peace policy who called him a "traitor" and even portrayed him in one notorious poster as a Nazi.
Rabin's widow Leah called Netanyahu the "architect of incitement" whose rhetoric fostered the climate for Rabin's murder by a right-winger opposed to his peace moves.
Following the asssassination, Israeli politicians turned down the volume on the rhetoric -- until recently.
"The shock of the assassination was such that people avoided anything that might sound offensive," said David Bar-Illan, Netanyahu's communications chief.
"But like anything else, once the shock wore off, things returned to what passes for 'normal' and of course it's very unfortunate," he told Reuters.

Bar-Illan said he was puzzled by the base level of political discourse in Israel, a country where the number of books bought per capita is said to be the highest anywhere and academia and cultural pursuits are both held in high regard.
That said, Sara Netanyahu's outburst did not fit the category of political debate, Bar-Illan insisted, even if the prime minister's office did issue an apology.
"This is a woman who feels besieged and blew up at what she considered very unfair, personal and unacceptable questioning," Bar-Illan said.
Veteran political correspondent Shimon Shiffer, who writes for Israel's popular daily Yedioth Ahronoth, doubted the first lady's latest blow-up would harm Netanyahu's political future.
But it was a public relations disaster for Israel's leader.
"His closest advisers said what she did was a catastrophe. They don't know how and where to bury themselves," Shiffer said.
